name: Bismuth

discovery.discoverer: Known since the 15th century, long confused with lead and tin

occurrence: Found natively and in sulfide/oxide ores, often as a by-product of lead, copper, and tin refining.
majorUses: Pepto-Bismol and other stomach-soothing medications (bismuth subsalicylate)
Low-toxicity replacement for lead in solder, fishing weights, and ammunition
notableCharacteristics: For decades believed to be the heaviest stable, non-radioactive element, until 2003 measurements revealed it's actually extremely weakly radioactive, with a half-life over a billion times the current age of the universe.
ncertRelevance: longest measured half-life of any radioactive isotope
whyHere: Bismuth's position at the very edge of nuclear stability means its main isotope decays, but so unbelievably slowly (a half-life over a billion times the universe's age) that it behaves as effectively stable for every practical chemical purpose.
didYouKnow: Synthetically grown bismuth crystals form strikingly colourful, geometric, staircase-like structures purely from how the metal cools and oxidizes — a favourite among crystal-growing hobbyists precisely because it's non-toxic, unlike most heavy metals.
genZNote: Technically radioactive but with a half-life longer than the universe is old, so basically not your problem. Also grows the prettiest rainbow crystals.
